title: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
authors: Naji Alazhar; Wassel Alazhar
abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. title: DuoRate: Two-Rate Per-Expert Precision Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Serving
authors: Mengqi Guo; Zhe Wei; Yuan Yuan; Jiunn Bin Lim; Boyi Pan; Michael Bi Mi
abstract: Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint pays for every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step pays only for the experts it selects. These are two different rate functionals over the same per-expert widths, yet published per-expert MoE allocators constrain only the first. We call the difference the store-read gap; in the released BitsMoE checkpoint, 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) of storage become 7.50 bpw of decode traffic. We propose DuoRate, which stores once and reads per workload. Offline, it stores one uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream and bakes a distortion tensor. A deployment therefore keeps a single artifact that prefill reads at the stored rate and decode reads at the workload's own rate. title: KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
authors: Taiga Ikeda; Daisuke Miyashita; Jun Deguchi
abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache-aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross-document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG-style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV-Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token-level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval-kv-repurpose.

title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
authors: Ze-Wei Liou; Harris Nover; Amey Naik; Andrii Skliar; Igor Shovkun; Ido Shahaf; Tri Dao
abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. title: Sampling-based Kinodynamic Planning with World Models
authors: Yitian Gao; Hanlan Yang; Zachary Kingston
abstract: Visual world models predict the consequences of actions from images, but planning with them is typically done by optimizers such as CEM and MPPI. However, these optimizers stall on long-horizon tasks where progress requires motion the objective does not reward, such as moving around a block before pushing it. This paper revisits kinodynamic sampling-based motion planning for world models, using the learned model as the propagator of a tree search in latent space. Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model, where they rapidly expand through intermediate states that myopic optimizers never sample. We present two exploration strategies for the high-dimensional latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE, with GPU-native batched expansion for efficient device utilization. We evaluate with an off-the-shelf DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task. Our approaches match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at up to 13.8x lower planning time in simulation, and improve the success rate by 20% on the real robot.

title: LeapBot-JAC: Joint Action Chains for World Action Models
authors: Chenhao Zhu; Baibing Liu; Pei Liu; Rui Yang; Lang Zhang; Mingyue Feng; Yaonong Wang; Jun Ma
abstract: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host's visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host's world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3% success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0% and 97.3%. On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5% to 70.4% and from 73.1% to 77.3%, respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget.

title: VFold: Symmetry-Aware Cross-Layer Value Cache Compression
authors: Neha Verma; Sungwon Kim; Kenton Murray; Kevin Duh
abstract: While caching key-value (KV) states accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) decoding, this cache can dominate memory usage at long context lengths. One solution is to compress this memory by exploiting inter-layer cache similarities. However, most existing techniques necessitate architectural changes to LLMs and incur substantial overhead. In this work, we propose a symmetry-aware value cache merging strategy that reduces cache memory while avoiding both harmful performance degradation and architectural overhead during decoding. title: Neural expectation-maximization and meta-models
authors: Zhuolin Fu
abstract: We interpret Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid probabilistic-inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) with Expectation--Maximization (EM). We show that self-attention implements a differentiable approximation to max-product LBP on an input-conditioned, dynamically structured MRF, with attention weights encoding learned structural affinities. We further establish an EM correspondence at the level of depth: each layer updates latent representations in an E-step-like forward pass, while the transition $θ^{(l)} \to θ^{(l+1)}$ across layers acts as an implicit M-step. Building on this interpretation, we introduce \emph{meta-models}, a design paradigm in which inputs generate instance-specific parameters, unifying mechanisms such as self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units within a single framework. Empirical results support the proposed perspective.

title: RouterInterp: Understanding Superposed Specialisation in Mixture of Experts Routing
authors: Ilya Lasy; Nora Yinuo Cai; Kola Ayonrinde
abstract: Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) models scale more efficiently than dense models by routing tokens to modular expert networks that are only active for processing a fraction of tokens. title: Secure Speculative Decoding for Large Language Models
authors: Yichi Zhang; Zhiqi Wang; Neil Gong; Yuchen Yang
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates inference for a large language model (LLM), referred to as the \emph{target model}, by first using a smaller model, referred to as the \emph{draft model}, to generate candidate tokens and then verifying them with the target model for acceptance or rejection. Prior studies primarily focused on the efficiency-utility trade-off of speculative decoding, e.g., lossy speculative decoding, leaving its security implications largely unexplored. In this work, we bridge this gap by providing the \emph{first} systematic study of the security implications of speculative decoding. Through a large-scale measurement study, we reveal a pronounced security-utility asymmetry: across a wide range of lossy speculative decoding methods, improvements in inference efficiency come at a disproportionately high cost to security, with attack success rates for jailbreak and prompt injection attacks increasing much faster than utility degrades. We then propose SecureSD, a new theory-guided speculative decoding method that enhances security while maintaining efficiency and utility.
